Dave:

I don't think either of these ideas sound familiar, they are not part of
our standard discussion of chi-square tests. In your first case (sum of
chi-square greater than or equal to number of bins): when the test
statistic equals the degrees of freedom p=0.50, so your describing a
situation where test statistic equals df+1 which might not be strong
evidence to suggest poor fit. Second rule (no chi-sq component exceeds
1) this will place you close to the result of your first rule which
would also provide some support for the fit of the model in question.

roblem is that you have too few detections, so that the chi-sq goodness-of-=
fit test has low power. In that case, if your distance data are not groupe=
d, you still have the Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cramer-von Mises tests, though=
their power isn't likely to be a whole lot better.

Hi Steve,

Thanks for the reply. Here's an example that I think illustrate what I mean.

We have 2089 detections with distances collected in 4 intervals (0-50,
50-100, 100-200, 200-300 metres). Since our distance data are grouped, the
KS and CvM tests are not an option.

I am fitting a half normal key function with automatic selection of simple
polynomial adjustments:


Model 3
Half-normal key, k(y) = Exp(-y**2/(2*A(1)**2))
Simple polynomial adjustments of order(s) : 4, 6
Results:
Convergence was achieved with 36 function evaluations.
Final Ln(likelihood) value = -2894.8067
Akaike information criterion = 5795.6133
Bayesian information criterion = 5812.5469
AICc = 5795.6250
Final parameter values: 105.98892 -1.4968388 18.497826
** Warning: Parameters are being constrained to obtain monotonicity.
**

Likelihood ratio test between models 2 and 3
Likelihood ratio test value = 64.5628
Probability of a greater value = 0.000000
*** Model 3 selected over model 2 based on minimum AIC



Here's the output from the "Detection Fct/Global/Chi-sq GOF test" results
page:



Cell Cut Observed Expected Chi-square
i Points Values Values Values
-----------------------------------------------------------------
1 0.000 50.0 611 584.44 1.207
2 50.0 100. 466 469.76 0.030
3 100. 200. 484 566.54 12.026
4 200. 300. 528 468.26 7.621
-----------------------------------------------------------------

No Degrees of Freedom for the test. No test possible.



In this case, no Chi-square test was possible due to having too few distance
intervals or equivalently too many parameters in the model, right?

I'd still like to be able to judge the fit of this model. I know I can
visually examine the detection probability plot, but what I'm wondering is,
in general, can I infer anything from the "Chi-square Values" column in the
table, even though no test was possible?

Thanks!

Dave

--
Dave Fifield
da...@mun.ca

-----Original Message-----
From: Stephen Buckland [mailto:st...@st-andrews.ac.uk]
Sent: February 14, 2012 05:26
To: Dave Fifield; DISTANCE...@JISCMAIL.AC.UK
Subject: RE: [DIST-SAMP] Goodness of fit assessment with insufficient
degrees of freedom

Dave, I'm not sure what the issue is. What do you mean by 'too few' df?

You only need 1df to get a valid chi-sq goodness-of-fit test. If you have
lots of detections, that test should have reasonable power for detecting
goodness-of-fit. If you have 0 df, then you should get a perfect fit
because you have fitted the maximum number of parameters possible. A more
likely problem is that you have too few detections, so that the chi-sq
goodness-of-fit test has low power. In that case, if your distance data are
not grouped, you still have the Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cramer-von Mises
tests, though their power isn't likely to be a whole lot better.

Steve Buckland

Dave, the only reason that you're not getting a perfect fit is the monotoni=
city constraint. In your example, you have many more detections in the 4th =
interval than the 3rd one, even though they're the same width. I would conc=
entrate on why that is happening - eg because observers record animals beyo=
nd 300m as if they were in band 4. Having a band 5 for >300 could resolve =
that. The fact that models with less than the max possible number of parame=
ters - and hence at least 1 df - fit badly tells you all you need to know a=
bout model fit.

Steve
